title: Epigenetic Editing Could Wipe Out Chronic Hepatitis B Infections - SingularityHub

analysis.time: The study was reported in October 2026, with results from a Phase 1/2 clinical trial in mice and monkeys, and a mention of the first human patient being treated in an ongoing trial earlier this year (N1, N18).
analysis.location_and_population: The research involved mice and monkeys as experimental models, and the treatment is being tested in humans, particularly those with chronic hepatitis B (N12, N14, N15, N18).
analysis.event: Scientists developed an epigenetic silencing approach to target HBV DNA in infected mice and monkeys, which could potentially replace daily antiviral pills for chronic hepatitis B (N12, N14, N15, N17).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The treatment showed promising results in mice, with 90% maintaining undetectable viral load after six months. It also demonstrated safety in monkeys with no notable side effects. The potential impact includes helping millions with chronic hepatitis B and addressing the risk of liver cancer and cirrhosis associated with HBV (N14, N15, N23, N24, N27, N28).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The team stopped short of calling it a cure, and the treatment is still in an ongoing Phase 1/2 clinical trial. The approach is considered a potential breakthrough but requires further testing in humans (N16, N18).

analysis.brief_en: A groundbreaking study published in October 2026 by SingularityHub highlights a new epigenetic editing approach that could potentially eliminate chronic hepatitis B infections. The method, developed by nChroma Bio and collaborators, targets HBV DNA in infected mice and monkeys by adding chemical tags that switch the genes off without altering the viral DNA itself. After three monthly doses, approximately 90% of the mice showed no signs of the virus for at least six months, and safety tests in monkeys found no notable side effects. The treatment, called CRMA-1001, uses a modified version of the CRISPR-Cas9 system to deliver genetic instructions for DNA methylation, primarily targeting the liver. While the team did not call it a cure, the results suggest it could replace daily antiviral pills for chronic hepatitis B. The approach also has potential for treating other stubborn viruses. The first human patient was treated in an ongoing Phase 1/2 trial, and further research is needed to confirm its effectiveness in people. The method addresses both forms of HBV DNA—cccDNA and integrated DNA—which are known to evade treatment and contribute to liver damage and cancer risk.
